extracted.intended_audience: fiction and nonfiction writers seeking developmental editing or evaluating sample developmental edits; authors considering hiring an editor or doing a self-directed developmental pass
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging and applying developmental-edit examples and for running a developmental revision pass on fiction and nonfiction manuscripts. Covers scene-, chapter-, and manuscript-level criteria, editorial commentary style, and measurable outcomes to expect from a true developmental edit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural changes over surface fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Developmental editing rebuilds the foundation of your story rather than focusing on commas and typos (copyediting). Strong sample edits should show structural moves: chapters relocated or compressed, whole scenes cut, subplots removed, or nonfiction chapters split.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for examples that move chapters around, cut whole scenes, or rebuild an argument. Examples include: three chapters compressed into one tight scene; a flashback moved from chapter two to chapter eight; an entire subplot removed because it pulls focus from the main story; a nonfiction chapter split in two because it tried to cover too much. These demonstrate 'real developmental thinking' rather than line-level polishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing (one of the Big Four)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pacing problems show up as sections where nothing happens or where everything happens too fast. Developmental edits should demonstrate how to spread tension across scenes and manage rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong example will re-balance scenes so conflict is spread (not all action packed into one chapter while others stall), create breathing room between intense moments, compress or expand beats for momentum, and use techniques like starting in medias res and compressing time. Quick tests: highlight first five sentences — who wants something right now? If not, move closer to the first decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character motivation (one of the Big Four)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must act with believable, clearly communicated reasons; actions should arise from motivation rather than plot necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good edits point out 'puppet-string' moments where characters act because the plot needs them, and show how to add or clarify motivations so choices feel earned. Techniques include: show motivation through action beats, redistribute backstory to moments of pressure, and consolidate character roles so motivation and consequences are clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot logic (one of the Big Four)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot logic is cause-and-effect: events should follow from established skills, clues, or prior actions rather than coincidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong examples remove coincidences, strengthen causal links, and show how clues are earned (e.g., protagonist finds crucial clue by using a skill introduced earlier). Editor comments should point to weak causal links and propose concrete fixes to chain events logically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader engagement (one of the Big Four)
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagement arises from stakes and investment: the reader must care what the characters want and what they risk losing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developmental edits should show how to make stakes clear and escalate them. Examples include making a goal concrete on-page, making the risk personal and urgent, and ensuring the opening promises a continuing engine that keeps readers turning pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial thought process revealed (marginal commentary & pattern recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best developmental examples include marginal comments that explain why changes are suggested, show pattern recognition across the manuscript, and balance critique with encouragement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for margin notes that do more than 'cut this paragraph' — they should explain effect (e.g., 'this backstory slows momentum right when tension should build'), identify repeated problems across chapters, and offer constructive alternatives. Tone should protect confidence (praise what works) while pointing to needed structural changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction developmental criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction-focused developmental checks: is the protagonist pursuing a specific want, do obstacles escalate logically, are choices believable, and does the ending pay off setup promises?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good edit will ensure opening scenes establish desire+problem quickly, reorder or cut scenes so each forces a choice, tune dialogue and beats to reveal character, and restructure acts (midpoint, escalation, climax) so the climax is earned. Use 'scene test' and 'stakes ladder' to ensure each scene contributes to the spine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonfiction developmental criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonfiction developmental checks: clear thesis, logical organization, evidence that supports main points, synthesis in the conclusion rather than mere summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should produce a one-sentence thesis, reorder material so each paragraph has a clear job, move strongest evidence forward, anticipate and answer the main counterpoint, and conclude with actionable next steps. Developmental moves include splitting overloaded chapters and reorganizing argument flow for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurable improvements demonstrated
rubrics_metrics.description: Good developmental-edit examples quantify changes where possible (not just 'reads better').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for measurable gains such as: reduced time to establish the main conflict from three pages to three paragraphs; removed four unnecessary characters without losing key information; cut word count by 20% while increasing impact; reorganized the argument to bring strongest evidence forward. Concrete metrics show the editor's effect on story economy and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning signs of weak examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators an example is NOT a developmental edit: focuses mainly on grammar/punctuation, word-choice tweaks without structural context, stylistic changes that reflect editor preference rather than reader need, small scene adjustments that don't change story, or revisions that change the writer's voice or intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hiring based on samples that are essentially copyediting or that remake voice. A developmental sample should preserve the author's voice while improving structure and reader experience; if the revised version sounds like a different writer, treat that as a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve author voice while improving reader experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Developmental editing should improve clarity, pacing, and stakes without making every manuscript sound the same or erasing authorial voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good edits 'reveal the stronger story inside the draft' so the writer thinks 'yes, that's what I was trying to say.' Look for edits that keep both versions sounding like the same writer while the revised version better serves readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening-scene checklist & techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific criteria for openings: open in medias res, show over tell, smart placement of information, start close to the first decision, establish a character, a problem, and a hint of the larger engine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical checks: highlight the first five sentences — who wants something right now? Circle every noun that describes weather/setting/backstory and cut until action breathes. Find the first refusal or obstacle and aim to start within a page of that refusal. Ensure the opening has one job: make a promise and pull readers into motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue & character-development rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should avoid naming emotions; instead show feeling through beats and choices. Scenes should give each character a private goal and a physical task to enforce conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put something concrete on the table (a key, contract, clock). Make goals clash and allow refusal. Replace lines that name emotions with physical beats or choices. Create distinct voices via vocabulary, sentence length, response style, and pet moves. Use exercises: write each character's one-sentence goal, add a task, remove explicit emotion labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonfiction argument structure and flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonfiction needs a spine: a sharp thesis in one sentence, two-to-four key points each supported by evidence, an anticipatory counterpoint and response, and a clear call to action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a pyramid: Thesis (one sentence), Point 1 with evidence, Point 2 with evidence, Point 3 or case, Counterpoint and response, Call to action. Order reasons logically (strongest-first or building to decision). Pair every point with concrete proof (numbers, dates, named sources) and end with a next step and measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene-level reconstruction rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: Each scene must have: an immediate want, a concrete obstacle, escalating stakes, a forced choice, and a change in the story state. Scenes should be 'load-bearing' not decorative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic questions: What does the protagonist want right now? What specific obstacle blocks them? What do they risk losing? What choice do they face? How are they different at the end? Techniques: start mid-conflict, compress time, build through obstacles, use silence, end with action. Scene test: if you cut the scene, would the story break?

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript-level plot & structure standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscript-level edits build a 'spine' (one-sentence), ensure a clean cause-and-effect chain, consolidate/merge redundant characters, place a public deadline or clock, and rebuild midpoint and climax so outcomes are earned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical moves: write a spine statement (Protagonist wants X; antagonist blocks with Y; loss equals Z). Mark act breaks and ensure each scene forces a decision or consequence. Merge characters who serve the same purpose. Add a public deadline (hearing, vote, delivery) to focus momentum. Track measurable changes (word count, chapter count, POV heads) and ensure every chapter ends on a decision, revealed consequence, or problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial letter & revision-process standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong editorial exchange includes a concise editorial letter with global feedback (structure, character arc, stakes, POV, theme, pacing), prioritized revision steps, a marked manuscript with margin comments, and a clear revision timeline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision priorities often run: rebuild the spine; scene triage (goal/conflict/outcome); midpoint choice; consolidate roles; prep for line work. Provide wins to protect (scenes/lines that must remain). Use a timeline of passes (Pass 1: structure; Pass 2: character & stakes; Pass 3: pacing & promise) and deliver a marked copy plus a change log so the author can track reasons and roll back if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marginal comments style (praise + prompts, not prescriptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Margin notes should balance praise with firm direction; ask questions and prompt alternatives rather than issuing commands that rewrite voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: praise sensory wins and point to where to tighten; flag low-heat exchanges with instructions to replace or cut; suggest micro-actions. Use queries and prompts ('What changes by the end of this exchange?') rather than rephrasing the author's line. Guard voice by asking to flag slips, not rewrite the voice entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-Job Test
rubrics_metrics.description: Every scene or paragraph should do at least two jobs (fiction: move plot and reveal character; nonfiction: make a claim and give evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot name two jobs for a unit, fold it into a nearby scene/paragraph or cut it. This prevents padding and keeps each unit 'load-bearing.' When rebuilding, state each character’s immediate want, add a concrete obstacle, raise stakes, and force a choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse outline & scene-audit method
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a reverse outline (one line per chapter/scene: location, purpose, outcome) and audit each unit for who drives the scene, goal, conflict, stakes, and change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag flat beats (no goal, no pressure, no change). Use the chain test (insert so, but, therefore between outcomes) to confirm cause-and-effect. Turn recurring problems into a fix list (merge scenes, add midpoint pressure, cut redundant characters) and record choices in a change log.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality benchmarks & exit criteria before line editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards to meet before moving to line-editing: a clear spine statement, every scene changes something, stakes appear by chapter 3 and rise by the midpoint, the lead makes hard choices, stable POV, appropriate word count, and no orphan subplots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exit criteria: no open high issues in a tracker; two fresh readers rate pace and clarity ≥4/5; word count within genre norms; a current style sheet; a completed read-aloud pass with stumbles fixed. When these checks pass, move to line and copy edit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick diagnostic checks and small exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical, repeatable checks to run quickly on openings, scenes, dialogue, and arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: highlight first five sentences and check for immediate want; circle setting/backstory nouns and trim; find first refusal/obstacle and start nearby; write a one-line thesis for nonfiction and turn main points into topic sentences with evidence; for dialogue, write each character's private goal and add a physical task; print a scene list and draw arrows for cause-and-effect (no arrow = no scene). Use these to triage pages fast.
